caption:
Welcome to my mini series on “ Investing for beginners”. Today we’re covering what a stock is and why people buy stocks. 

A stock is a tiny piece of ownership in a company.
So when you buy a share of a company, you’re not just buying a random number on an app…you actually own a very small part of that business.

People buy shares because they believe the company will grow and become more valuable over time. If it does, the price of their shares may increase, but some companies also pay shareholders a portion of their profits through dividends.

It’s important to know that stocks can go up and down, and returns are never guaranteed…. And in part 2 (tomorrow) we’ll go over why people invest and what beginners should do.

caption:
I grew up in a low-income family, so when I started making good money in my late 20s, I honestly went through a phase where I wanted to buy all the things I never had… including this Gucci diaper bag that cost almost $3,000.

At the time, I didn’t think it was a bad decision since I had the income, I wasn’t going into debt, and I genuinely loved it…But looking back, this bag taught me one of the biggest money lessons of my adult life: lifestyle creep.

If you’ve never heard of it, lifestyle creep is when your income goes up and your spending quietly follows. Things that once felt crazy expensive start to feel normal.

That’s exactly what happened to me. One day you’re excited about a $50 purchase, and the next you’re convincing yourself a $3,000 diaper bag makes total sense. And honestly? I still use this bag almost every day….So this isn’t a post about regretting it.

It’s about realizing that building wealth isn’t just about earning more money. It’s also about keeping your expenses in check as your income grows.

Because if every raise turns into a bigger mortgage, a nicer car, more shopping, or more expensive habits, it’s really hard to get ahead.

This diaper bag ended up being a pretty expensive lesson, but it helped shape how I think about money today.

These days, I’m much more focused on building wealth than looking wealthy.

Anyone else have a purchase that taught them a major money lesson? 👇

caption:
Life insurance can feel way more confusing than it needs to be.

Term life insurance covers you for a set period of time, like 10, 20, or 30 years. It’s usually cheaper and is meant to protect your family during the years they’d need it most — mortgage, young kids, debt, daycare, etc.

Whole life insurance is permanent coverage. It usually costs a lot more, but it can make sense for high-net-worth families, estate planning, business owners, or people who have already maxed out other investment options.

There is a lot of marketing right now pushing whole life insurance to parents with young kids, but on average, term life is usually the better fit for most young families.

Not financial advice, but please do your due diligence before signing anything. Ask questions, compare quotes, and make sure you understand what you’re actually buying.

*not saying whole life insurance is a scam BUT that advertising to young vulnerable families that it is the best type of insurance for them is shady*

We divided things into areas:
• finances
• groceries
• meals
• kids logistics
• household purchases
• cleaning

• shared grocery list on our phones
• autopay for bills
• rotating meals
• alternating daycare drop-offs
• subscribe & save for household items

It’s definitely not perfect, and some weeks one of us still does more than the other.

Let’s be honest - we’ve all been there when we’re exhausted at night and trying to figure out how to make more money so we can stay home with our kids. 

The thing is  ChatGPT can give you 100 business ideas in seconds but it can’t tell you which problem you understand deeply, which skill people already trust you for, or what your capable of doing with kids around. 

Instead of asking AI to build your entire business, ask yourself:

What do people already come to me for?
What problem have I solved in my own life?
What could I package into a service, guide, template, product or community? 

You’d be surprised how many things you can come up with if you start searching for businesses ideas in your everyday life. 

Instead of asking “What business should I start?”

Ask: 
-What services are currently in demand in my city that I could start with less than $1,000?

-have experience in ___, people often ask me for help with ___, and I can work ___ hours a week. What could I offer?

When I say “budget,” I’m not talking about guessing or cutting lattes…
I mean understanding your real monthly cash flow

👉 Take your after-tax household income (what actually hits your account)
👉 Subtract your actual monthly expenses

What’s left is what tells you if this is doable.

✔️ Positive → you likely have room to make it work
➖ Break-even → you’ll need to tighten spending or increase income
❌ Negative → this is where most families are right now… and it just means there’s a gap to solve

Living on one income in Canada is tough but not impossible. 

You either:
– reduce expenses
– increase income
– or do both

caption:
Most people don’t think about layoffs… until it’s too late.

I was recently featured in the @globeandmail talking about how Canadians are preparing… but honestly, there are a few things I wish more people knew ahead of time.

If I thought I might get laid off, here’s what I’d focus on first:

• Build a real emergency fund (not just “a few thousand”)
• Understand how EI actually works (there can be delays + gaps)
• Don’t rely only on work benefits (they can end fast)
• Know your severance rights — don’t just accept the first offer
• Reduce fixed expenses NOW, not when you’re already stressed
• Consider a second income stream (even a few hundred/month helps)

Layoffs don’t just affect your income…
they impact your savings, your confidence, and your timeline.

I was laid off many years ago and it really opened my eyes up to how much I didn’t know. Last year when my company was going through layoffs, I knew how to be prepared. Funny enough, I actually started this account right after I signed my termination agreement!

caption:
Most parents aren’t taught this about formula prep 👇

❌ Incorrect prep
Powder first → then water → shake hard

Why this isn’t ideal:
• Adding powder before water can affect the correct dilution (water-to-formula ratio). 
• Shaking creates excess bubbles.
• More bubbles = more swallowed air = more gas or fussiness for some babies.

It seems small, but little details matter with tiny tummies.
⸻

✅ Correct prep
Water first → then measured powder → gently swirl

How to do it:
1️⃣ Add the exact amount of water first (always follow your formula’s instructions).
2️⃣ Add properly measured scoops.
3️⃣ Swirl or roll gently instead of aggressively shaking.
4️⃣ Let it sit a few minutes so bubbles can settle.

This keeps the ratio accurate and helps reduce air in the bottle.
⸻

🍼 Ready-to-Feed vs Powder

• Ready-to-Feed (RTF) is the most sterile option and there’s no mixing. It’s often recommended in the first 2–3 months, especially for newborns, premature babies, or babies with weaker immune systems.
• Powder formula is commonly used after the newborn stage for healthy full-term babies. It’s more cost-effective but requires careful preparation because powder is not sterile.
• Some specialty formulas are only available in powder form in Canada (like nutramigen) so may be used earlier with your doctors guidance. Always consult your doctor if you’re unsure which is best for your baby.
⸻

🧴 Packed vs Unpacked Scoops

Not all formula scoops are the same.
• Most formulas require a level, unpacked scoop (fill and level off — do NOT press it down).
• Some formulas specifically say lightly packed scoop.

🍼What about anti-colic bottles?
If your baby struggles with gas, bottles designed to reduce air intake (like vented or anti-colic systems such as @drbrowns style bottles) can sometimes help by minimizing swallowed air during feeds

Always check what YOUR can says. Different formulas have different densities, so one scoop is not universal.
⸻

Every brand has slightly different instructions. This post is educational — always follow your formula container and your healthcare provider’s guidance.

Save this for 3am feeds 🤍
And send to a parent who might not know.

How to actually do this (Canada) 👇

If pregnancy makes working impossible, you may qualify for EI sickness benefits before maternity leave.

Here’s the simple breakdown:
1️⃣ Get a medical note from your doctor, OB, midwife, or NP stating you’re unable to work for medical reasons
2️⃣ Stop working (your employer submits your ROE to Service Canada)
3️⃣ Apply online for EI sickness benefits — you can receive up to 26 weeks
4️⃣ When baby arrives, switch to maternity + parental leave as planned (your time off is not reduced)

This is not early maternity leave — it’s sickness benefits before mat leave starts.

caption:
It cost us $7,463.11 for 7 days at Royalton Splash Riviera Cancun flying from Toronto with a baby and toddler.

That total included flights, hotel, taxes and fees.

Here’s the breakdown:
• 2 adults: $5,130
• 1 child: $555
• Infant: $0
• Taxes & fees: $1,778

Almost $1,800 of that was just taxes and fees — something families don’t always factor in when budgeting.

So… was it worth it?

What we liked:
• No cooking, no planning meals
• Everything walkable
• Easy beach + pool access
• Nighttime kids activities (face painting, foam parties, bubbles, dance shows) — huge hit
• Built-in entertainment every day

What we didn’t like: 
• The splash park is a big selling point, but the main slides are 4+ and toddlers can’t use them
• Restaurants felt understaffed with long wait times 
• Food sometimes came out cold 
• Rooms were not properly cleaned 
• Many visibly sick kids during our stay
• We heard multiple families mention norovirus going around

Thankfully, we didn’t get sick, but there was a clear understaffing issue and questions about hygiene and food safety. 

Overall? We had fun. The kids enjoyed it. It was convenient.

But if I’m being honest — for toddlers specifically, I’d probably try a different resort next time that’s more age-focused, less crowded, and focuses more on food safety and hygiene.

caption:
Bonding with a baby isn’t about how many hours you’re home.It’s about how predictable you are when you are.

Babies don’t understand time the way adults do. Their brains attach through patterns — the same person, the same routine, repeated again and again.

That’s why attachment forms through repetition, not availability.

This is what that often looks like:
A dad who works long hours but consistently owns one small moment.
•Morning wake-up routine (same order every day: cuddle, light on, song, get dressed)
•After-work reconnection (first 5 minutes home = hug, sit on the floor, quick check-in)
•Bath or bedtime routine (bath, lotion, teeth, hair — calm and predictable)
•One daily question (same question every day: “What was the best part of today?”)
•Weekend anchor (Saturday morning breakfast, walk, or errand that’s always yours)

That routine becomes familiar. Familiar becomes safe. Safe becomes connection.

For many families, one parent holds most of the structure of the day, while the other anchors a specific moment within it. Both roles matter. One doesn’t replace the other — they strengthen each other.

If you’re trying to build this kind of bonding, here’s what actually works:
• Pick one daily moment and protect it
• Keep the routine simple and repeat it the same way
• Be fully present (no phone, no multitasking)
• Let your child associate you with that moment

Even 5–10 minutes, done consistently, builds trust.

What’s the one moment your kids associate with you?

If you’re quietly paying for fertility treatment in Ontario 🤍 please read this.

Starting in 2025, there’s a new Ontario Fertility Treatment Tax Credit that can give you up to $5,000 back.

But here’s the part that can trip people up:

You can only claim what you actually paid out of pocket.

If insurance reimbursed part of your treatment, that amount doesn’t count. Only the unreimbursed portion qualifies.

So if you paid $16,000 and insurance covered $9,000, you would claim the remaining $7,000.

The credit is 25% of eligible expenses (up to $20,000), and it’s refundable — meaning you can still receive money back even if you don’t owe taxes.

We were easily wasting $1,000/month without realizing it.

Here’s exactly what we did to save (as a Canadian family):

1.Re-quoted our home + auto insurance using alumni/professional discounts (CPA + university of Waterloo) → saved ~$90/month (@td_canada has alumni/professional rates yet most people don’t even check this)

2.Switched our main credit card to @amexcanada for groceries + more→ now getting $$ back in points on spending we were already doing

3.Cut just ONE Uber Eats order/week → saved ~$300–$350/month without feeling restricted

4.Groceries: Costco for bulk + @nofrillsca or Freshco for weekly grocery shopping → cut ~$200/month vs shopping only at Loblaws/Fortinos

5.Bought discounted gift cards at @costco_canada or @amazonca (Uber Eats, clothing stores, restaurants) → instant ~20% savings on things we already buy

6.Used Amazon Subscribe & Save strategically → ordered once for the discount, then paused so it doesn’t auto-renew

7.Switched to a no-fee bank + high-interest savings and stopped paying ~$15/month in fees and actually earned interest (@tangerinebank / @simpliifin are popular for no-fee banking, as well as @wealthsimple)

8.Automated savings on payday → we save first instead of hoping there’s money left

9.Set a weekly “spend limit” for random purchases → way easier than tracking a full month

10. 10-minute weekly money check → caught subscriptions, double charges, and random Amazon spend early

These weren’t extreme measures but small steps that can add up!

caption:
Starting the milk and egg allergy step ladder with my baby was one of the scariest things I’ve done as a mom.

If your baby has a milk allergy or egg allergy, you’ve probably been told about the “allergy step ladder” — but no one really explains what it actually looks like in real life.

Here’s how we’re reintroducing milk and egg safely at home (with guidance from our allergist):

• We start with baked milk and baked egg in small, controlled amounts
• We increase slowly only if there are no symptoms (hives, vomiting, swelling)
• We space exposures properly instead of rushing the ladder
• We never introduce new foods on the same day
• We keep antihistamines and our emergency plan ready

For us, even a crumb of egg muffin can cause hives — so this process feels huge.

If you’re navigating:
– baby milk allergy
– egg allergy reintroduction
– food allergy anxiety
– the allergy step ladder process

You’re not alone. I’ll be sharing exactly what’s working (and what’s not) as we go 🫶🏼

caption:
What no one tells you before applying for maternity leave in Canada 🤍

There are legal ways to protect your income and extend your time off — but most of us only learn them after we’ve already applied… when it’s too late to change things.

Here’s what I wish someone had told me:

• If pregnancy complications make working impossible, you can take up to 26 weeks of EI sickness benefits before maternity leave — without cutting into your time with baby
• If your baby is in the NICU, you may qualify for the Family Caregiver Benefit — again, without reducing your maternity leave time
• EI doesn’t withhold enough tax — but you can plan for this and avoid the tax shock
• Choosing 12 vs 18 months isn’t just about time off — it affects your cash flow and when you’ll need daycare
• Your first EI payment is often 4–6 weeks late — you need a buffer
• Self-employed moms must register for EI special benefits at least 12 months before claiming

No one explained any of this to me (and more) when I needed it most.

So I put everything I learned into one step-by-step Maternity Leave Guide so other moms don’t have to do this the hard way 🤍

Starting solids can feel like a lot.
There’s so much advice out there and most of it makes it feel more complicated than it needs to be.

If you’re about to start, here’s what actually matters:

• Your baby shows signs of readiness (around 4–6 months)
• You choose an approach that works for you (purées, BLW, or a mix)
• You focus on safe textures + supervision
• You introduce allergens early and consistently

You don’t need the perfect plan or fancy meals.
And you definitely don’t need to get everything “right” from day one.

Most babies learn through exposure, repetition, and time—not perfection.

This guide walks you through the basics so you can feel more confident and less overwhelmed when you start.

caption:
No one actually prepares you for maternity leave in Canada… especially the money part.

Here’s what I wish I knew before I applied:

• You do not get your full salary
• EI is based on your average weekly earnings before leave (so any unpaid sick days or reduced hours can lower it)
• Choose 12 months even if you plan to stay home 18 — the total amount of EI is the same, the 18-month option just stretches it thinner
• Your first payment can take 4–6 weeks to start — plan for that gap
• If your employer offers a top-up, you may need to return for a certain period or repay it
• EI doesn’t withhold enough tax, so some moms end up owing at tax time — setting aside a small amount monthly helps
• If you worked overtime/bonuses before leave, those help your EI average — sometimes it’s worth maximizing earnings before your claim starts
• If pregnancy complications push you off work early, ask about sickness benefits first — it can extend how long you’re paid before maternity leave kicks in
• You can only change from 12 to 18 months once at the very beginning — after that, it’s locked

No one explained any of this to me until I was already on leave and trying to figure it out on my own.

I share real, clear breakdowns like this so you don’t have to learn the hard way.

⠀

If your baby has reflux, eczema, mucousy or bloody poop, or cries after every feed… it might not be “just a phase.”

Cutting dairy (and sometimes soy) changed everything for us.
